newsitem.title: CHINA: Shenzhen stock market surpasses China rival.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen stock market surpasses China rival.

text.p: The Shenzhen stock exchange has confounded widespread uncertainty over whether it would survive the return of neighbouring Hong Kong in 1997 to become China's top bourse, analysts said on Wednesday.

Trading volume on the Shenzhen stock exchange is now regularly double that of the Shanghai exchange, a dramatic turn-around from a year ago when people in the markets were asking whether Shenzhen had a future at all.
In the first nine months of 1996, Shenzhen's stock turnover hit 574 billion yuan ($69.16 billion) against Shanghai's 483 billion yuan, exchange figures show.
"The most important factor is high expectations of good opportunities for Shenzhen after Hong Kong's takeover," said a senior stock analyst with China Guotai Seucurities.
"Investors believe Shenzhen will gain the most of any Chinese city from the takeover because it is the Chinese city nearest to Hong Kong," he said.

This year, the underdog has surpassed its big brother, the Shanghai stock exchange, in share price gains and turnover because an improvement in China's economy has benefitted firms listed there more than those in Shanghai, traders said.

By Wednesday's close, Shenzhen's composite index had rocketed 215 percent to 346.54 points against its close on the last trading day of 1995, compared with its Shanghai counterpart, which rose 88 percent to 1010.834 points.
Traders said the increases in Shenzhen shares were led by local real estate and transportation firms, indicating a belief that the Hong Kong takeover would benefit these sectors first.
In addition, Shenzhen has a bigger proportion than Shanghai of property and light industrial firms listed, which tend to be more sensitive to the performance of the economy, they said.
The rise of shares of such firms on the exchange have contributed to the bull run this year, they said.
Analysts also pointed to Beijing's promise of a grace period for Hong Kong to keep a capitalist system after the takeover.

"This will effectively stop Hong Kong funds from flowing directly into mainland markets and vice versa," said a second analyst with Shenyin and Wanguo Securities. "Shenzhen will be a springboard and this will provide huge chances for the market."
Analysts agree China's economy has entered its best period since 1993, with annual retail price inflation expected at below seven percent this year, down from 14.8 percent in 1995.

"There will be no big change in the trend (of Shenzhen leading Shanghai) at least for the rest of this year," the Guotai analyst said. "Shanghai has tried very hard to retake the lead but has not succeeded."

On the record trading volume day on October 14, stock turnover on the two exchanges was 23 billion yuan (about HK$21.41 billion), three times the turnover on the Hong Kong market that day. Of this figure, Shenzhen's turnover was 14 billion yuan and Shanghai nine billion yuan.
